cues.text: The Poor Man's Lawyer
Born Mark Roy in 1577 at Sigmaringen, in Swabia, Fidelis studied philosophy and law at Freiburg im Breisgau, earning doctorates in canon and civil law.
He traveled through France, Italy, and Spain as tutor to a young nobleman before establishing himself as a practicing lawyer.
He became known for his particular dedication to defending the poor without payment.
Leaving Law for the Cloister
Increasingly troubled by the corruption he witnessed in the legal profession of his day, Fidelis abandoned his practice and was ordained a priest.
He immediately entered the strict Capuchin reform of the Franciscan order at Freiburg in 1612, taking the religious name Fidelis.
A Preaching Mission to the Grisons
Fidelis quickly became recognized for his preaching and his tireless efforts against the spread of Calvinism, writing (always anonymously) numerous pamphlets defending Catholic doctrine.

In 1621 he was appointed to lead a Capuchin mission to the canton of the Grisons in Switzerland, a region that had largely turned Protestant, tasked with bringing its people back to the Catholic faith.
Suspected of Political Motives
Fidelis's mission met with such notable success — converting several important local leaders — that alarmed Protestant preachers began spreading rumors.
They claimed his true purpose was political rather than religious, portraying him as an agent preparing the region for subjugation by Catholic Austria.
Hostility toward him and his fellow Capuchins grew steadily throughout the winter and spring.
A Foretold Martyrdom
Fidelis had long confided to companions his hope of dying for the faith.
Before returning to the Grisons in spring 1622, he preached a farewell sermon at Feldkirch.
There, he stated plainly that he expected his labors to end soon in martyrdom.
Re-entering the region, he was met everywhere with cries of 'Death to the Capuchins!'
On April 24, 1622, while preaching at Seewis, an armed band burst into the church, dragged him from the pulpit, and killed him with repeated blows.
Legacy
Fidelis's relics were later translated to Chur and then to Feldkirch, with the transfer to Chur in 1622 and the subsequent transfer to Feldkirch in 1628.
Canonized in 1746, he is remembered as the protomartyr of the newly founded Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith .
He is also remembered as the protomartyr of the Capuchin order's missionary reform—a lawyer whose defense of the poor gave way to a still more radical gift of his own life.
